summary: Describes the state of standardization of Internet protocols as determined by the Internet Architecture Board. It is a periodically reissued list of protocol statuses. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1610.

eli5.summary: A report card listing which rules of the Internet are official and which are still being tried out. A newer report card replaced it.

questions: internet official protocol standards list march 1994
how does the ietf standards process work
subtitle: The official record of Internet protocol standards and their standardization status.

tldr.problem: The Internet protocol landscape was evolving rapidly in 1994, and developers needed a current, authoritative source listing which protocols were standards, which were experimental, and how each fit into the standardization process.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1600 provides the official list of Internet protocols organized by maturity level (Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Informational, Historic, and Obsolete) and requirement level (Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use, Not Recommended), explaining the standardization process and the meaning of each category.
tldr.outcome: This 1994 edition was replaced by RFC 1610 as the standards landscape continued to change. It is now Historic.

today: RFC 1610 replaced this document. RFC 1600 is Historic and documents the state of Internet standards as they existed in March 1994.

sections.title: The Internet Standards Registry
sections.content:
RFC 1600 is the Internet Architecture Board official publication of Internet protocol standards. It explains both the standards process and lists protocols at each stage of standardization, serving as the authoritative reference for what constitutes an Internet standard in March 1994.

Unlike earlier versions, this edition adds an Obsolete category alongside Historic to better track protocols that have been formally replaced or withdrawn. The document reflects an Internet that had grown substantially, with standards covering applications, networks, management, security, and many other areas.
sections.eli5: In 1994, the Internet was growing fast and had many protocols. This official list told engineers which protocols they had to use, which were recommended, which were experimental, and which were too old. It introduced a new category called Obsolete for protocols that had been replaced.

sections.title: Maturity Levels and Requirement Levels
sections.content:
A protocol maturity level describes its standardization state. Standard protocols are officially approved by the IESG and assigned STD numbers. Draft Standard protocols are under active consideration, likely to advance within six months unless major objections are raised. Proposed Standard protocols are candidates for future standardization and require at least two independent implementations before advancing. Experimental and Informational protocols document research or external work. Historic protocols have been superseded or abandoned. Obsolete protocols have been formally replaced.

The requirement level is independent and indicates deployment expectations. Required protocols must be implemented in all systems. Recommended protocols should be implemented. Elective protocols are optional. Limited Use protocols apply only in special circumstances. Not Recommended protocols should generally be avoided.
sections.eli5: Each protocol has two labels. One shows its stage: Standard (done), Draft Standard (almost done), Proposed Standard (being reviewed), Experimental (research only), Informational (from elsewhere), Historic (old), or Obsolete (replaced). The other shows how important it is: Required (everyone needs it), Recommended (you should add it), Elective (your choice), Limited Use (special cases), or Not Recommended (avoid it).

sections.title: The Path to Standardization
sections.content:
The standards track is the formal process by which protocols advance from proposal to standard status. The IESG, the steering group of the IETF, manages this process. A protocol enters the track as a Proposed Standard, marking it as a candidate for eventual standardization. It must remain proposed for at least 6 months and demonstrate at least two independent implementations before advancing to Draft Standard.

From Draft Standard, a protocol must wait at least 4 months and show operational experience with demonstrated interoperability between multiple implementations before the IESG recommends advancement to Standard. The entire process typically takes a year or more. Protocols can exit the track into Experimental status if deemed not ready, or move to Historic or Obsolete status if they become outdated.
sections.eli5: Getting a protocol standardized takes time and proof that it works. Proposed Standard is step one and lasts at least 6 months. Draft Standard is step two, also at least 4 months. Standard is the final step. At each step, you must prove the protocol works in the real world and that at least two different implementations agree.

sections.title: The Obsolete Category
sections.content:
Unlike earlier editions, RFC 1600 introduced an Obsolete category separate from Historic. Historic protocols have been superseded or abandoned but are still documented as part of the standards record. Obsolete protocols have been formally withdrawn or replaced. This distinction helped developers understand whether a protocol had a known replacement or was simply no longer in use.

By 1994, the standards system had matured enough to handle both the growing number of protocols and the need to clearly track which ones had been formally replaced with newer versions.
sections.eli5: The 1994 version added a new category called Obsolete. Historic means old and not used. Obsolete means it was formally replaced with something better. This helped engineers know which protocols to switch to.

sections.title: The 1994 Protocol Landscape
sections.content:
RFC 1600 captured the state of Internet standardization in March 1994, a period of explosive growth and commercial adoption. The document listed protocols across applications (mail, naming, file transfer, remote access), transport (TCP, UDP, SCTP), network (IP, IGMP, ICMP), and management (SNMP, MIB) layers.

RFC 1610 replaced this edition with the next quarterly update. RFC 1600 is now Historic but documents an important snapshot of the Internet standards as they existed in early 1994.
sections.eli5: In 1994, the Internet had many more standards than in 1993. This list showed what was official and how important each protocol was. A newer version replaced it, but RFC 1600 shows what the Internet looked like at that moment in time.
